Find the direct primary study and report experimental model, comparator (quiescent/nonproliferating cells or other cell types), methylation result, and evidence supporting or refuting selective increase.'}

The direct primary study is PMID 10727665 (Cardiovascular Research, 2000). It compared human aortic smooth muscle cells in normal aortic tissue (in situ, contractile) with the same cells explanted and cultured in vitro (dedifferentiated, proliferating). The ESR1/ERα promoter appeared unmethylated in normal aorta but became methylated in the cultured proliferating cells.

The authors’ assays included Southern blot, COBRA, and RLGS-M. RLGS-M suggested the change was selective at the gene/locus level—ESR1 and a limited set of CpG-island genes—rather than a generalized rise in methylation, and did not appear to require heightened methyltransferase activity. The study compared cell states, not different cell types, so it supports selective methylation changes within aortic smooth muscle cells but does not establish specificity relative to other cell types. The available evidence is from the abstract; full text was unavailable.

The primary study directly answers the question: ESR1 promoter methylation was absent or undetectable in normal aortic tissue and present in proliferating cultured human aortic smooth muscle cells. I’ll check the evidence graph for existing records before adding the result.

Yes. The primary study (PMID: 10727665) found that the estrogen receptor-alpha (ESR1/ERα) promoter was apparently unmethylated in normal, in situ human aortic smooth muscle cells but became methylated after explantation and proliferation in culture. Southern blot, COBRA, and RLGS-M analyses supported a selective locus-level methylation change rather than a generalized increase in methylation.

However, “selective” referred to particular genomic loci; the study did not establish specificity compared with other cell types.

FINAL DECISION: YES
